title: Songs in the Night: Elihu on Unanswered Cries
summary: Elihu takes up Job's complaint that righteousness brings him no benefit. He points Job to the heavens: God is so high that human sin cannot harm him and human righteousness cannot enrich him. People cry out under oppression, but often they cry only for relief and never ask, “Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night”; such empty pleas go unanswered. Job's impatient words, Elihu concludes, are the same empty talk.
story: This short chapter is Elihu's third speech, sandwiched between his long defense of God's justice (chapter 34) and his final hymn to God's greatness (chapters 36 and 37). Here he answers two things Job has said: that he is more righteous than God (as Elihu hears Job's protest) and that it gains him nothing to avoid sin. Eliphaz had made a similar point earlier, asking whether a man can be of use to God (22:2-3), but Elihu develops it toward a different question: why do so many cries of the suffering go unanswered? His answer, that they are cries for relief rather than cries for God, prepares for the moment when God will answer Job, not with relief first, but with himself.
historical:
Like the rest of the dialogue, this chapter is set in the book's patriarchal world beyond Israel's borders, and it stands apart from any datable event. Its concern with oppression, though, reflects the lasting social reality of the ancient Near East. Most people lived close to subsistence, and the arm of the mighty (verse 9) was a real force: landowners, creditors, officials, and raiders could strip families of land and livelihood with little recourse. Job himself had described such oppression vividly in chapter 24.

Elihu doesn't deny that oppression is real or that the oppressed cry out. His claim is narrower and sharper: many who cry out under injustice seek escape from their suffering without seeking the God who made them. That observation isn't tied to any one century. It reflects the long experience of wisdom teachers across Israel and its neighbors, who noticed how often prayer in trouble is a demand for rescue rather than a turning toward God.
cultural:
Two ideas common in the ancient world shape the chapter. The first is that the gods need something from human beings. In Mesopotamian myth, humanity was created to relieve the gods of labor and to supply them with offerings, so that the gods depended in some sense on their worshipers. Elihu, like the rest of the Bible, rejects this. God is above the clouds; human sin cannot damage him and human goodness cannot supply a need he has. Our wickedness and righteousness matter chiefly to other people, to a man like yourself (verse 8).

The second is the practice of crying out. In Israel and the wider region, a cry for help was a formal appeal, made to a king, a judge, or a god, and a just ruler was expected to hear it. Elihu contrasts that raw cry with the prayer of someone who asks where God is and remembers that God gives songs in the night. Night was a time of danger and fear in a world without artificial light, and a song in the night meant confidence given in the dark, not after it has passed.
literary: The speech has a simple frame. Verses 2 and 3 restate Job's position, verse 4 announces a reply to Job and his friends, and verse 16 closes with a verdict echoing the end of chapter 34: Job multiplies words without knowledge. Between them are two movements. Verses 5 to 8 argue from the height of the heavens that God is beyond human harm or gain, using carefully balanced if-clauses. Verses 9 to 15 turn to unanswered prayer, contrasting the cry for relief with the question no one asks. The phrase “songs in the night” is the chapter's most memorable image, and its placement in the middle gives the short speech its center.

outline.t: God above the clouds: human sin and virtue cannot touch him
Cries for relief that never ask for God

doctrines.note: God is self-sufficient. He is not harmed by human sin or enriched by human righteousness, and he gives rather than receives. This does not make human conduct unimportant; it means God's commands serve our good and our neighbor's, not his need.

Elihu distinguishes a cry for relief from a turning toward God the Maker. His point is not that God ignores the suffering, but that prayer which seeks only escape, and never God himself, has missed what prayer is.
God teaches human beings more than the beasts and makes them wiser than the birds. People are creatures, but creatures made to know their Maker and to be taught by him.

words.note: Zamir, song. The word belongs to the vocabulary of music and praise and is related to the verb used for singing to God and to the word for psalm. In verse 10 God is the one who gives songs in the night, joy or confidence granted in the middle of darkness. The phrase has become one of the best-loved lines in the book.

Ashuq, oppression. The word refers to extortion and the crushing of the weak by the strong. Its appearance in verse 9 shows that Elihu takes the suffering of the oppressed seriously, even as he questions the prayers they offer.

Shav, emptiness or vanity. In verse 13 God does not listen to empty pleas, cries that are hollow at the center. It is the same word used in the commandment against taking the LORD's name in vain (Exodus 20:7).

Hevel, breath or vapor, and by extension vanity or futility, the key word of Ecclesiastes. In verse 16 Elihu says Job opens his mouth in hevel: his words are vapor, insubstantial against the reality of God.

christ: Elihu insists that God needs nothing from us, and that is true; the New Testament says the same (Acts 17:25). The surprise of the gospel is what this self-sufficient God chooses to do. He doesn't stay above the clouds, untouched by human sin. In Jesus he enters the world, bears the sin that Elihu says cannot harm him, and is himself the one whose cries under oppression seem to go unanswered. The link to this chapter is thematic rather than predictive. But the God who gives songs in the night is shown most clearly in the Son who sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed (Mark 14:26) and who, in his own darkest hour, still prayed to God as his God.

hard.q: If God is not affected by our sin or righteousness, does it matter to him how we live?
hard.a:
Elihu's argument could be heard as saying that God is indifferent, but that isn't his point, and it isn't what the rest of Scripture teaches. Elihu is answering a specific claim: that Job's righteousness ought to have earned him something from God, as though God were in Job's debt. His reply is that God cannot be put in anyone's debt. He gains nothing from our goodness and loses nothing by our sin.

The Bible as a whole holds this alongside another truth: God is grieved by human sin (Genesis 6:6) and delights in those who fear him (Psalm 147:11). These aren't signs of need but of love. God is not diminished by our wrongdoing, yet he cares about it because it harms the people he made and the relationship he intends. Elihu captures the first half of that picture; the rest of the Bible supplies the second.

questions: Elihu says many cry out for relief but never ask, “Where is God my Maker”. What would it look like for your prayers in hard times to seek God himself and not only a way out?
What might a song in the night look like in your life, or in the life of someone you know who has suffered?
If God gains nothing from your goodness, why do you think he still commands it? Whose good does it serve?
